name: Crystagen
summary: A three-amino-acid peptide (Glu-Asp-Pro) from Russian 'bioregulator' research, promoted to support immunity in older people; evidence is mainly the developers' own small studies.
what_it_is: Crystagen is a lab-made chain of three amino acids, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and proline (Glu-Asp-Pro, or EDP), from Vladimir Khavinson's peptide research in Russia. Its developers patented it as an 'immunogeroprotector', meaning a substance meant to slow the age-related decline of the immune system. In their lab and rat studies it boosted the growth and maturation of immune cells and helped protect the thymus, the gland where T cells mature.

evidence.why: Rat and cell studies plus small studies in older adults with no randomization described, all reported by the developers in a patent and a review.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; not on FDA compounding lists
status_us.note: Crystagen is not an FDA-approved drug and appears on none of FDA's compounding lists (nominated substances, updated May 2026; safety-risk and withdrawn nominations, April 2026). FDA allows pharmacy compounding only from ingredients that are in an approved drug, meet a USP standard, or are on or under review for its bulk list.

benefits.claim: Immune blood tests returned to normal in more older adults with weakened immunity when it was added to standard care (82% vs 56%)
Less fatigue and weakness reported by older adults taking it
Less shrinking of the thymus, with its structure better preserved, in rats after radiation
More growth of thymus and spleen tissue from old rats, and more immune-signaling activity by cells from aging mice, in lab culture

risks.risk: No independent human safety data; reports of no side effects come from the developers
Because it is meant to stimulate immune cells, it could in theory worsen autoimmune disease or work against anti-rejection drugs
No FDA-approved or pharmacy-compounded version exists, so the identity and purity of products are unverified

avoid_if: Autoimmune disease, an organ transplant, or taking immune-suppressing medicines, unless a clinician is involved
interactions: Immune-suppressing medicines: could in theory work against each other (not studied)

before: Complete blood count with a white-cell breakdown
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for Crystagen; the developers judged its effects with immune blood tests, which a clinician could repeat if there is a reason to.

studies.title: Peptide substance revealing an immunogeroprotective effect, pharmaceutical composition on its base and the method of its application
studies.people: 70 older adults with weakened immunity after environmental radiation exposure: 38 treated, 32 on standard care
studies.finding: Immune measures returned to normal in 82% of treated people versus 56% of controls, with no side effects reported. The patent does not describe randomization or blinding.

studies.title: The Use of Thymalin for Immunocorrection and Molecular Aspects of Biological Activity
studies.people: Older adults, rats and cell cultures (the developers' studies)
studies.finding: Summarizes the developers' work: the tripeptide EDP (crystagen) improved immune test results and fatigue in older adults, protected the thymus in irradiated rats, and slowed the growth of a leukemia cell line in culture.

ask_your_clinician: Do I actually have weakened immunity, and what is causing it?
Could this affect any immune condition I have or medicine I take?
Which vaccines or proven steps would protect me more?

notes_for_editor: Identity comes from the developers' 2021 review ('tripeptide EDP (crystagen)') and their US patent claiming H-Glu-Asp-Pro-OH; NLM MeSH lists Glu-Asp-Pro only as 'T-36 tripeptide', without the trade name. The human data (82% vs 56% immune normalization in 70 older adults) appear only in the patent and the developers' review, with no randomization or blinding described and no independent replication. Russian regulatory status was not confirmed.
